messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan had always been drawn to the fast-paced world of journalism, but it wasn't until he started working as a reporter that he met his ex-partner, Alex. At first, their relationship seemed perfect - they shared a passion for storytelling and were each other's biggest supporters. But behind closed doors, Alex's controlling behavior and physical abuse slowly eroded Rohan's sense of self-worth. The memories of those violent incidents still felt like they were happening in the present moment, rather than something that was over. When they resurfaced, Rohan would feel overwhelmed by emotion, forced to stop whatever he was doing as the pain and fear washed over him. He couldn't shake the feeling that his body was reliving the trauma all over again - the same physical pain in the same parts of his body. Rohan's job required him to take public transportation, but ever since the abuse, riding the bus made him anxious. Being alone with men, especially if they resembled Alex, triggered a cascade of negative thoughts and memories. He would start dwelling on what he had done wrong, replaying every conversation and argument in his head, convinced that he was somehow to blame for the abuse. This self-blame rumination became a maladaptive coping mechanism - it allowed him to momentarily escape the pain, but ultimately reinforced his feelings of inadequacy. As Rohan navigated his daily life, he began to notice that even small delays would send his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. When something took longer than expected, he assumed something bad was happening, and his body would tense up in anticipation. At night, he'd wake up multiple times to check whether he was safe, as if the threat of harm was always lurking just out of sight. Rohan's experiences had taught him that people couldn't be trusted - not even himself. He began to see the world through a lens of fear and mistrust, constantly on high alert for potential dangers. Even when his current partner or friends reassured him that he was safe, Rohan struggled to believe it. His mind would always find ways to rationalize why they were wrong. As the memories continued to haunt him, Rohan started to restrict his food intake as a way of coping with the emotions. He'd undereat, hoping that by controlling one aspect of his life, he could somehow regain control over the rest. But this only served to reinforce his feelings of inadequacy and shame. Rohan's partner noticed the changes in him - the weight loss, the anxiety, the constant checking - but Rohan couldn't bring himself to talk about it. He was convinced that he was broken beyond repair, that no one could ever truly understand what he'd been through. It wasn't until Rohan's editor expressed concern about his declining performance and increasing absences that he realized he needed help. The memories were still present, the triggers still potent, but Rohan finally acknowledged that he couldn't continue living like this. He began to see a therapist, hoping to find a way to break free from the cycle of negative thoughts and emotions that had consumed his life. As he sat in the therapist's office, Rohan's eyes would dart around the room, checking for potential threats, still trying to convince himself that he was safe. But with each passing session, he slowly started to confront the memories, the triggers, and the negative appraisals that had held him hostage for so long. He began to see that his experiences didn't define him - that he was more than just a victim of abuse. With time, Rohan hoped to rebuild his sense of self-worth and learn to trust himself and others once again.
